title: Is Angi Worth It for Contractors? Real Cost Per Job (2026)
desc: Is Angi worth it for contractors? What Angi, HomeAdvisor and Thumbtack leads really cost per booked job in 2026, and what to build instead.

blocks.h1: Is Angi worth it for contractors? *The real cost per job.*
blocks.lede: Angi can be worth it for a new contractor who needs work fast and can call every lead within minutes. For most established contractors it stops being worth it, because each lead is shared with several competitors and the real cost per booked job ends up many times the price on the invoice. Here is how to check your own numbers, and what to build instead.
ticks: The cost per job sum, with a worked example
What to do instead of renewing

blocks.html:
Is Angi worth it for contractors?

Sometimes, but rarely for long. Angi (which now includes HomeAdvisor's lead service) sells you the contact details of homeowners asking for a quote. You pay for each lead whether or not you win the job, and the same homeowner is usually sent to several other contractors at the same time.

That model works for some businesses: a new crew with an empty calendar, a trade with big ticket jobs, or an owner who can answer every lead inside five minutes. It works badly for contractors who are already busy, who quote large jobs that take hours to price, or who cannot drop tools to call back straight away.

The only honest way to answer the question for your business is to work out what one booked job costs you, not one lead. The rest of this guide shows you how.

How much do Angi leads cost in 2026?

Angi does not publish a price list. What contractors report, and what most industry guides repeat, is roughly this:

  • Lead price: about $15 to $85 per lead, and over $100 for high value trades like roofing in busy markets.
  • Membership: an annual fee, commonly around $300 a year, on top of the leads.
  • Contracts: many pros sign up on a yearly agreement with a set lead budget, so check the renewal date and cancellation terms before you sign.

Thumbtack works a little differently. You set your own budget and the most you are willing to pay per lead, and you are charged when a customer contacts you, even if they never hire you. Pros report anywhere from about $10 to over $100 per lead depending on the trade and market.

Why the price per lead is not your real cost

The number on the invoice is the cost of a phone number, not the cost of a job. Three things push the real figure up:

  1. The lead is shared. Industry write ups report the same Angi lead going to three to eight contractors at once, and roofers report up to sixteen. You are buying a seat at an auction, and the homeowner usually picks the first to call or the cheapest.
  2. Many leads never answer. Contractors describe homeowners who were only browsing, numbers that are disconnected, and people who got their quote from someone else before you called.
  3. Quoting takes time. A site visit, measuring and pricing a big job can take hours. If you lose most of those quotes, that time is a cost too.

One HVAC owner described the problem in a widely upvoted Reddit thread: roughly $3,400 spent, about 60 leads, and 7 jobs closed, with the same leads going to four other companies. That works out to about $486 per booked job, before counting a single hour of quoting.

The sum to do before you renew

Open your Angi or Thumbtack billing history for the last three to six months and work out two numbers:

  • Cost per booked job = total spent on the platform ÷ number of jobs you actually won from it.
  • Profit per job = what you typically make on one of those jobs after materials and labour.

If the cost per booked job eats a big share of your profit per job, the platform is renting you work at a loss. A quick way to see it: a $50 lead at a 20% close rate costs $250 per job. The same lead at a 10% close rate costs $500.

$1,000204$250

$3,400607$486

Then ask one more question: how many of those customers would you have won anyway through referrals or Google? Those jobs should not count in the platform's favour.

When a lead platform is worth it

Lead platforms are not always a bad deal. They tend to pay off when:

  • You are starting out, have no reviews yet and need jobs on the calendar while you build a name.
  • Your average job is large enough that one win covers months of lead costs.
  • Someone in the business can call every lead back within minutes, every day.
  • You use it to fill quiet weeks and pause it when you are flat out, instead of leaving it running all year.

Many contractors on Reddit describe exactly that path: use the platform to get off the ground, then drop it once referrals and reviews carry the business.

What to do instead: own your leads

The advice that comes up again and again in contractor forums is to stop renting leads and start owning them. A lead you own comes to you only, so you are not racing four other companies to the phone. In practice that means:

  1. A complete Google Business Profile. It is free, it puts you on Google Maps, and homeowners check it before they call. Our Google Business Profile checklist walks through every setting.
  2. A steady flow of Google reviews. Text a review link to every happy customer the day the job is finished, including the ones who found you on Angi.
  3. Your own website. A fast site with a page for each service and area, real job photos and a tap to call button turns searches into calls that nobody else gets. See what a trade website needs.
  4. Referrals on purpose. Ask every good customer, and look after the builders, designers and property managers who can send you repeat work.

None of these cost you per lead, and they keep working after you stop paying. That is the real difference between renting work and building a business that brings it in.

How to leave Angi without losing work

  • Check your contract first. Find your renewal date and cancellation terms so you are not charged for another year.
  • Build the replacement before you switch off. Get your Google Business Profile and website working a few weeks ahead.
  • Turn platform customers into reviews. Every job you won through Angi can become a Google review that brings the next customer to you directly.
  • Track where calls come from. Ask every new customer how they found you, so you know what is working.

items.q: Is HomeAdvisor the same as Angi?
items.a: HomeAdvisor's lead service now sits under Angi, which is why contractors often call it Angi Leads. The way it works is the same: you pay per lead, and leads are usually shared with other pros.

items.q: How much does Angi charge contractors?
items.a: Angi does not publish a price list. Contractors commonly report about $15 to $85 per lead, more for trades like roofing, plus an annual fee often around $300.
Usually not. Standard leads are commonly sent to several contractors at once, so speed and price decide who wins the job.

items.q: Is Thumbtack better than Angi for contractors?
items.a: Thumbtack gives you more control over your budget and the maximum you pay per lead, but you still pay when a customer contacts you, whether or not they hire you. Do the same cost per booked job sum for both.

items.q: Can I get a refund for a bad Angi lead?
items.a: Angi lets eligible pros request credits for some problems, such as invalid contact details or leads outside your service area. Contractors often report that requests are declined, so keep records of every bad lead.

items.q: What is the best alternative to Angi?
items.a: For most contractors, leads they own: a complete Google Business Profile, steady Google reviews, a fast website with a page for each service, and referrals. They cost nothing per lead and nobody else gets the same customer.
